issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe intrusive, sensory-dominated, repeatedly replaying trauma memories. That combination is not impossible, but with no other items indicating organized narrative access, the 'very easily' wording pulls in the opposite direction and is clinically inconsistent within this node.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of mugging/robbery. 'Being around children' and 'Happy families' do not show a plausible thematic link to the reported trauma, and there are no accompanying threat or appraisal items to explain why these social/family cues would specifically trigger this patient's robbery-related PTSD.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: 'I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation mainly links triggers and memory with maladaptive strategies, but the actual triggers and memory content given are socially/family themed and intrusive-image based; deliberate conflict-seeking does not fit clearly with those items and looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, triggers centered on children and idealized families are hard to link clinically unless there is additional trauma meaning not represented elsewhere. The memory items describe perceptual re-experiencing of the robbery, but these triggers imply family/child themes that are absent from the rest of the profile, making the trigger set feel disconnected from the trauma type.

Within the Triggers node, 'children present' and 'happy families' suggest a loss/family-comparison theme, whereas 'being criticised or corrected' suggests interpersonal shame or sensitivity. These could coexist, but together they do not form a coherent trigger pattern tied to a robbery, especially given no threat or appraisal items supporting these meanings.

'Happy families' is a weakly plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery trauma and is hard to connect to the accompanying memory items, which are purely sensory/reliving-based and suggest trauma reminders tied more directly to the event. It does not fit well with the otherwise robbery-linked trigger pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers and memory to maladaptive strategies, but the selected triggers and memory items imply intrusive re-experiencing, for which suppression/avoidance is coherent; deliberate conflict-seeking appears clinically disconnected and unusually externalising relative to the rest of the profile.

vignette: Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a hairdresser, styling the hair of his clients with precision and care. But on that fateful evening two years ago, everything changed. As he walked home from the salon, lost in thought about a particularly difficult haircut he had struggled with earlier that day, he was suddenly grabbed from behind and dragged into an alleyway. The assailants, two young men, demanded his wallet and phone, and when Kofi hesitated, they punched him in the face, leaving him dazed and bleeding on the ground. The image of those few minutes is forever seared in Kofi's mind - a jumbled mix of sounds, smells, and visuals that he can't shake off. The smell of alcohol on his attackers' breath, the sound of their laughter as they ran away, and the feeling of helplessness as he lay there, unable to move or escape. Even now, whenever he catches a whiff of booze, Kofi is instantly transported back to that alleyway, his heart racing and his palms growing sweaty. In the aftermath of the mugging, Kofi became increasingly withdrawn, avoiding social gatherings and turning down invitations from friends and family. He couldn't bear the thought of being around people, fearing that they would judge him or criticize him for not fighting back harder. His wife, Ama, tried to be supportive, but even her gentle suggestions or corrections felt like a personal attack to Kofi, sending him spiraling into self-blame and rumination about what he could have done differently. As the days turned into weeks, Kofi found himself becoming more and more isolated, stuck in a cycle of negative thoughts that he couldn't escape. He would replay the events of that night over and over in his mind, trying to make sense of it all, but unable to find any answers. The memories were like a film playing on repeat, with no pause button or fast-forward option. And when Ama tried to talk to him about what happened, Kofi found himself struggling to put his thoughts into words, the emotions and sensations overwhelming him. At work, things began to suffer as well. Kofi's clients started to notice that he was distant and preoccupied, and some even complained about his lack of attention to detail. His usual precision and care were nowhere to be seen, replaced by a sense of detachment and disconnection. Ama encouraged him to seek help, but Kofi was hesitant, fearing that therapy would mean confronting the trauma head-on, something he wasn't sure he was ready for. But as the months went by, Kofi realized that he couldn't keep living like this - stuck in a state of hypervigilance, always on the lookout for potential threats, and unable to connect with those around him. The final straw came when Ama sat him down and told him that she felt like she was losing her husband, that the man she loved was disappearing behind a wall of fear and self-doubt. It was then that Kofi knew he needed help, not just for himself, but for their relationship as well. As he sits in the therapist's office now, Kofi is unsure of what to expect, but he knows that he can't keep running from his memories and emotions forever. He hopes that therapy will be a safe space for him to confront his fears and learn to manage his symptoms, so that he can start rebuilding his life and reconnecting with those around him. But most of all, he hopes that he can find a way to silence the constant replay of that night in his mind, and finally find some peace.
